sections.msg: Transport relies almost entirely on roads; international roads have been largely rehabilitated, while regional and local roads are deteriorating.

items.k: Share of passenger transport carried by road (freight: over 96%)
Length of public roads managed by the state
Share of regional and local roads in poor condition (2019)

paras.t: Road network size and condition
Public roads carry about 98% of passenger transport and over 96% of freight transport, moving up to 40 million tonnes of freight and 640 million passengers a year.
paras.b: Roads carry about 98% of passengers and over 96% of freight

paras.t: Roads and streets total about 34,000 km, of which 19,000 km are public roads managed by the Ministry of Transport and Communications: 4,326 km of roads of international importance, 5,335 km of national roads and 9,149 km of local roads.
paras.b: 19,000 km of public roads are managed by the state

paras.t: Of public roads, 7,580 km have hard surfaces (5,698 km asphalt concrete, 1,871 km black gravel, etc.). 9,388 km are gravel roads and 1,617 km remain unpaved. There are also 15,190 km of streets and roads belonging to cities, villages and enterprises.
The share of international roads in good condition rose from 21% (2010) to 44% (2019). Since 1997, 2,043 km have been rehabilitated with donor investment.
paras.b: International roads in good condition: 21% → 44%

paras.t: However, the share of international transport corridor roads in good condition fell from 68% (2015) to 58% (2019). Of 14,576 km of regional and local roads, 36% were in poor condition (2019), and the share in good condition fell from 32% (2015) to 24% (2020).
paras.b: 36% of regional and local roads are in poor condition

paras.t: Regional and local roads in poor condition grew from 2,186 km (2010) and 2,163 km (2015) to 5,210 km (2019), more than doubling in nine years. By road roughness, 46.5% of national roads are "poor".

The World Bank's infrastructure governance assessment states that road and rail density is low and lags neighbouring countries, and that much of the road network is of poor quality. In the 2019 Global Competitiveness Index, the country ranked 103rd of 140 for infrastructure and 129th for transport infrastructure.
In the World Economic Forum report, road quality ranked 113th of 141 countries.

From 2021 to 2024, freight volumes across all modes rose by more than 21%, and transport and storage services grew from 28.6 billion som to 46.8 billion som. Forty trade and logistics centres are in operation.
paras.b: Freight volumes rose by more than 21% in 2021–24

paras.t: As trade background, the OECD notes that precious metals accounted for 51% of exports in 2018, and that the share of (re-)exports to Russia rose from 14% (2018) to 19% (2023).
Freight flows and logistics
The main driver of logistics growth is the entry of international online marketplaces and the opening of their branches; more than 30,000 Kyrgyz sellers are registered, three times the 2022 number.

The OECD states that road is the main mode of transport, and that rail from the EU and Türkiye costs about the same as road but takes far longer. Half of survey respondents reported growing delays at the border with Kazakhstan, and queues of up to 400 trucks form in winter at the Caspian port of Aktau.
A 132,000 m² logistics hub (IBC Global Hub) on the outskirts of Bishkek is expected to be completed by the end of 2028. NDP 2030 states that 40 logistics centres are in operation.
The OECD states that about 3,500 km of roads were paved in the past four years.
There is a dual structure: international corridors are being rehabilitated with donor funding, while the domestic road network deteriorates for lack of budget.
paras.b: International roads improve while the domestic network deteriorates

sections.msg: Transport policy is structured as NDP 2030 Section 5.2 (Regional Hub) → the Concept for the Development of the Road Sector 2023–2030; the site's policy tree has no separate national plan for railways, aviation or urban transport.

fig.cap: Figure 1-2 Policy framework (status as of November 2026)

paras.t: Overarching plan: NDP 2030 Section 5.2 "Regional Hub" sets five targets: (1) 15 million tonnes of rail freight a year; (2) at least 1 million m² of warehouses and logistics facilities; (3) construction, reconstruction or repair of at least 50% of national roads; (4) USD 1.5 billion of value added in the transport sector; (5) 7 million airport passengers and 45,000 tonnes of air cargo a year.
paras.b: NDP 2030 Section 5.2: five targets including 15 million tonnes of rail freight and 50% of roads

paras.t: Long-term direction: the National Development Strategy 2018–2040 states that transport infrastructure will bring the country out of its "transport dead end" and make the Kyrgyz Republic a transit country with safe transit corridors for passengers and freight. It envisages a domestic railway network linking north and south, with public–private partnerships as the main instrument for projects in this area.

The same strategy calls for rehabilitating at least 550 km of trunk roads every year, of which at least 200 km should be domestic roads, and names toll road schemes and procurement of special equipment as sources of finance for maintenance and operation. For aviation, it calls for liberalising the Air Code, introducing the "fifth freedom", and making Manas Airport a transit cargo hub linking Southeast Asia and Europe.

The tasks of Section 5.2 are: reconstructing and building the road network (including the North–South road); the railway network (China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan railway, electrification); renewing urban transport (electric buses, charging network); civil aviation (airports, air traffic control); transport and logistics centres; and participation in international ports and routes.
paras.b: Six tasks: roads, railways, urban transport, aviation, logistics, international routes

paras.t: As international routes, Section 5.2 lists "Kyrgyzstan–China–Pakistan", "Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan–Turkmenistan–Russia" and "China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan–Turkmenistan–Iran", and calls for public–private partnerships and direct investment in port logistics and simplified trade and customs procedures. For building roads and transport hubs, it calls for creating conditions for investment agreements and public–private partnerships (PPPs).
Road plan: the Concept for the Development of the Road Sector 2023–2030 (Cabinet Resolution No. 71 of 10 February 2023). It replaced the previous Concept 2016–2025 (Government Resolution No. 372).
paras.b: Concept for the Development of the Road Sector 2023–2030

paras.t: As directions for reform, the Concept lists introducing market-based management mechanisms, strengthening the financial base for roads and introducing digital management. External funding for roads accounts for 35–48% of total external investment.

External funding for transport (state budget tables) was 5,471 million som (2018) and 8,971 million som (2022, approved), with 15,628 million som projected for 2024. Agricultural, transport, energy and water infrastructure account for 92.3% of public investment in 2023–2025.

Institutional arrangements in the Concept: the Roads Department of the Ministry of Transport and Communications sets policy; the ministry's Road Facilities Directorate acts as the client for road works and is responsible for construction, repair and maintenance; and the Land and Water Transport Department manages transit traffic.

On financing: the budget for road construction, repair and maintenance rose 7.7-fold in 2006–2010, improving the condition of more than 630 km of asphalt and black gravel roads, among others. Budget shortfalls persisted in 2010–2020. The Concept also cites the informal economy (more than 23% according to the National Statistical Committee) as a background factor in budget shortfalls.

The World Bank assessment estimates that roads, water and power need additional spending of 63% of GDP (2018) over 2019–2030, about two-thirds of it for roads. The national public investment programme amounts to only 3–5% of GDP a year.

The site's policy tree groups the Concept into five pillars: (1) roads of international importance; (2) national, regional and local roads; (3) bridges and tunnels; (4) maintenance and road safety; (5) institutions and finance.
paras.b: Five pillars of the Concept

paras.t: In road maintenance, 57 regional maintenance units and corridor organisations were merged into a single state enterprise (Kyrgyzavtozhol) with six regional branches, fully funded through annual contracts.
paras.b: Maintenance units were merged into a single state enterprise

paras.t: The CAREC material states that 57 regional maintenance units, four corridor organisations and the Bishkek–Osh road directorate were merged into one state enterprise, and that the former regional bodies became local offices of the road management department of the Ministry of Transport and Communications.
Note: the chapters of the Concept on targets, measures and expected results are on a paid site and have not been read. The Concept's numerical targets are therefore not covered here.

sections.msg: Only roads have a national plan; for four of the five NDP 2030 targets (railways, logistics, value added, aviation), the site's policy tree has no responsible plan.

fig.cap: Table 1-1 Subprogrammes (active cooperation by table row; overlaps included)

paras.t: The road Concept covers trunk roads and corridors, national and local roads, bridges, maintenance, and institutions and finance. Urban transport is said to be covered by "Smart and Sustainable City of Bishkek" to 2033, but its text has not been checked. Railways and aviation appear only in the text of NDP 2030.
paras.b: Only roads have a plan

paras.t: The weight of the NDP 2030 targets lies in railways, logistics and aviation, yet no national plan to elaborate them can be found. This is where the gap between targets and implementation is widest.
paras.b: Railways, logistics and aviation have targets but no plans

paras.t: According to the Concept, international roads were rehabilitated with donor funding, while national and local roads deteriorated amid persistent budget shortfalls. The domestic roads pillar (Pillar 2) and the maintenance pillar (Pillar 4) appear to be where the gap between plans and funding is widest.

The Concept lists ADB, EBRD, the Export-Import Bank of China, the World Bank, the EU, the Eurasian Development Bank, JICA, the Arab Coordination Group and others as financiers of international road rehabilitation since 1997.
paras.tnj: The Concept lists ADB, EBRD, the Export-Import Bank of China, the World Bank, the EU, the Eurasian Development Bank, the Arab Coordination Group and others as financiers of international road rehabilitation since 1997.

paras.t: In railways, the first railway public–private partnership (Karakol–Makmal) was signed with a US consortium in early 2025. In roads, the Uzgen bypass PPP will build more than 14 km of new road.

The World Bank assessment states that feasibility studies for PPP projects are optional, which can undermine quality, and that only USD 1 million of the USD 4 million project preparation fund has been used or committed. Public transport is one of three areas where PPPs are active.

sections.h: Overall: outlook for the five national targets
sections.msg: None of the five NDP 2030 targets can be tracked with annual international data; the only trackable international target, road traffic deaths, is off track.

fig.cap: Table 2-1 Gap to targets (actual pace = average change over the past five years; required pace = change needed to reach the target in 2030)

paras.t: The five targets of NDP 2030 Section 5.2 (rail freight tonnage, warehouse floor area, share of roads rehabilitated, transport value added, airport passengers and cargo) appear only in national yearbooks and announcements by the transport ministry and airport company; there are no figures the site can retrieve automatically each year.
paras.b: None of the five targets can be tracked annually

paras.t: International data on rail freight are in tonne-kilometres (to 2021) and air passengers cover Kyrgyz airlines only, so they use different yardsticks from the national targets (tonnes, and airport users including foreign airlines).

The current-situation passage of NDP 2030 gives the value of transport and storage services as 28.6 billion som (2021) and 46.8 billion som (2024). This is a different yardstick from the target of "USD 1.5 billion of transport value added", so progress cannot be read from it.

Of the five targets, 15 million tonnes of rail freight and 7 million airport passengers are large targets that depend on whether new railway and airport capacity is built. The 50% roads target depends on the volume of domestic road rehabilitation. Because none has annual results, delays cannot be spotted and addressed along the way.

Bringing road traffic deaths down to the benchmark of 8.4 requires a level about 30% below even the 11.5 of 2018. Few active projects have road safety as their main objective, so pairing road rehabilitation with safety measures is a challenge.

Road traffic deaths are 13.8 per 100,000 population (2023). Reaching the SDG benchmark of 8.4 (half the 2010 level) would require a fall of 0.77 a year, but over the past five years they have risen by 0.46 a year.
paras.b: Road traffic deaths: rising over the past five years

paras.t: The long-term strategy's "rehabilitation of at least 550 km a year" is a volume target alongside NDP 2030's "at least 50% of national roads", but no annual results are published for either. Simply publishing the length rehabilitated each year would make it possible to measure the gap to target.

sections.msg: International roads have been largely rehabilitated, but road traffic deaths have risen again since 2018 and domestic roads are deteriorating.

fig.cap: Figure 2-1 Road traffic deaths (dotted line = SDG benchmark)

paras.t: Trends and background
Trend: road traffic deaths fell from 16.8 per 100,000 population (2010) to 11.5 (2018), then rose to 13.8 (2023).
paras.b: Road traffic deaths 11.5 (2018) → 13.8 (2023)

paras.t: Road traffic deaths peaked at 21.0 in 2014 and fell sharply until 2018. Since then they have fluctuated between 12 and 14 and have not approached half the 2010 level of 16.8 (8.4).
By road roughness (IRI, International Roughness Index), 59.7% of international roads are good and 19.0% poor; for national roads, 24.1% are good and 46.5% poor.
paras.b: 46.5% of national roads are poor (IRI)

paras.t: Phase 2 of the Bishkek–Torugart road rehabilitated five sections, dividing sections with other development partners, and included a customs inspection facility in the plan.

On international roads, 2,043 km have been rehabilitated since 1997 and 900 km are covered by rehabilitation projects. Phase 2 of ADB's Bishkek–Torugart road (539 km, linking western China with Kazakhstan and Russia) was rated "successful" in its evaluation.

NDP 2030 lists improving road traffic safety among its public safety tasks. The pillars of the road Concept include maintenance equipment, measures against winter snowdrifts and avalanches, and road safety facilities.
Underlying causes
The road budget rose 7.7-fold in 2006–2010, but budget shortfalls persisted in 2010–2020. The Concept cites inefficient work planning as a cause of the budget shortfall.

The national target of "rehabilitating at least 50% of national roads" appears to target a domestic network in which more than 40% of sections are in poor condition. Without published annual rehabilitation results, progress cannot be measured.
paras.b: The 50% roads target cannot be measured without published results

paras.t: The transport section of the Digital Concept 2024–2028 lists a digital map of all roads, a road asset management system (RAMS) to plan maintenance budgets, automated quality monitoring of road construction and GPS on machinery, and automated weighing and measurement of freight vehicles. It states that weight control will remove corruption risks in enforcement and reduce road damage.

A road asset management system is the foundation for the "planning that includes life-cycle costs" called for by the World Bank assessment. Annual road condition data would also make it possible to measure progress on NDP 2030's "50% of roads".

The World Bank assessment states that life-cycle costs, including maintenance, are hardly considered at the project planning stage, and that the 2022 public investment management regulation (No. 714) does not require them either. In 2022, capital investment crowded out recurrent spending, leaving insufficient funds to operate and maintain existing assets.

Citing the Islamic Development Bank-financed rehabilitation of the Osh–Batken–Isfana road (170 million som), the same assessment expresses concern that rehabilitated roads again require external funding.

On procurement, the 2022 Law on Public Procurement excluded state and municipal enterprises from its scope, raising transparency concerns. The assessment recommends requiring life-cycle cost projections for all public investment and aligning sector investment plans with the medium-term budget.

The deterioration of domestic roads stems not only from the volume of funding but from a system in which funding is skewed towards new construction and rehabilitation and maintenance is deferred. Corporatising maintenance and including life-cycle costs in planning are the reforms that would advance the 50% roads target.
Related cooperation

Related cooperation: the trunk roads row has 18 projects worth about USD 365 million (JICA about USD 133 million, ADB about USD 130 million, Islamic Development Bank about USD 52.3 million, EBRD about USD 23.9 million, Japan (Embassy, etc.) about USD 16.5 million, Korea about USD 7 million). Korea's project is for road safety improvement (2026–2030).
paras.b: About USD 365 million in the trunk roads row
paras.tnj: Related cooperation: the trunk roads row has 18 projects worth about USD 365 million (ADB about USD 130 million, Islamic Development Bank about USD 52.3 million, EBRD about USD 23.9 million, Korea about USD 7 million, and others). Korea's project is for road safety improvement (2026–2030).
paras.bnj: About USD 365 million in the trunk roads row

paras.t: Main trunk road projects: JICA's International Trunk Road Improvement (about USD 85.1 million); ADB's CAREC Corridors 1 and 3 Connector Road (loan about USD 68.5 million, grant about USD 9.5 million, to 2027); the Islamic Development Bank's Susamyr–Talas–Taraz road Phase 4 (about USD 52.3 million, to 2027); ADB's Issyk-Kul Ring Road (Barskoon–Karakol, about USD 29 million and about USD 7.5 million, to 2033); and EBRD's Issyk-Kul Ring Road (about USD 23.9 million).
paras.tnj: Main trunk road projects: ADB's CAREC Corridors 1 and 3 Connector Road (loan about USD 68.5 million, grant about USD 9.5 million, to 2027); the Islamic Development Bank's Susamyr–Talas–Taraz road Phase 4 (about USD 52.3 million, to 2027); ADB's Issyk-Kul Ring Road (Barskoon–Karakol, about USD 29 million and about USD 7.5 million, to 2033); and EBRD's Issyk-Kul Ring Road (about USD 23.9 million).

paras.t: Maintenance and safety projects: Korea's road safety improvement on the Bishkek–Issyk-Kul road (about USD 7 million, 2026–2030); JICA's snowdrift countermeasures on the Bishkek–Osh road (about USD 7.4 million); JICA's road maintenance and paving equipment for Batken Region (about USD 5 million); and the EU's Kara-Balta–Chaldovar road (about USD 2.7 million).
paras.tnj: Maintenance and safety projects include Korea's road safety improvement on the Bishkek–Issyk-Kul road (about USD 7 million, 2026–2030) and the EU's Kara-Balta–Chaldovar road (about USD 2.7 million).

paras.t: Bridge projects: JICA's replacement of the Naryn River bridge on the Bishkek–Osh road (about USD 22.8 million, 2025–2032), and Japan (Embassy, etc.) and JICA's Urmaral River bridge on the Talas–Taraz road (about USD 16.5 million and about USD 12.8 million).
paras.tnj: Bridge projects consist of bridge replacements on the Bishkek–Osh and Talas–Taraz roads.

paras.t: Active funding is concentrated in international corridors and major tourist and regional ring roads, with few projects directly targeting regional and local roads, where many sections are in poor condition. Only one project, Korea's, has road safety as its main objective.
The bridges, tunnels and passes row has 4 projects worth about USD 52.1 million (JICA about USD 35.5 million, Japan (Embassy, etc.) about USD 16.5 million).
paras.b: About USD 52.1 million in the bridges row
paras.tnj: The bridges, tunnels and passes row has 4 projects worth about USD 52.1 million.
paras.bnj: About USD 52.1 million in the bridges row

sections.msg: Border crossing times have shortened, but logistics quality has declined since 2018, and railways, where new line construction has only just begun, are a gap in cooperation.

fig.cap: Figure 2-2 Logistics Performance Index and rail freight

paras.t: Trends and background
The Logistics Performance Index fell from 2.55 (2018) to 2.30 (2022) (out of 5).
paras.b: Logistics index 2.55 → 2.30

paras.t: Rail freight went from 738 (2010) to 1,003 million tonne-km (2021), rising and falling repeatedly.
Rail freight peaked at 1,010 million tonne-km in 2014, fell to 807 in 2016 and recovered to 1,003 in 2021. International data run only to 2021; later values appear only in national yearbooks.

Rail freight has not grown much in ten years, so NDP 2030's "15 million tonnes a year" appears to assume the opening of the China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan railway rather than an extension of current lines.
The World Bank assessment puts the country 108th of 160 on the Logistics Performance Index, with a score of 2.4 out of 5 for trade and transport infrastructure.

CAREC corridor measurements show road border crossing time falling by 24%, from 3.7 hours (2021) to 2.8 hours (2022). Border crossing costs, however, rose from USD 23 to USD 31. Exit at Torugart, at 50.1 hours (2022), was the longest delay, attributed to China's COVID-19 measures.
paras.b: Border crossing 3.7 → 2.8 hours; exit at Torugart 50 hours

paras.t: The cost of moving 20 tonnes of freight 500 km was USD 1,888 by road and USD 556 by rail (2022).
Speeds on CAREC corridors (excluding stops) were 51.8 km/h by road (2022), while rail rose from 21.2 km/h to 30.1 km/h. Rail border crossing time fell from 1.6 hours to 1.0 hour.

Delays by border: entry at Torugart rose from 2.3 hours (2020) to 5.1 hours (2022) and exit from 2.4 hours to 50.1 hours. The report attributes this to China's COVID-19 measures requiring trailers to be transloaded in the border buffer zone, and states that the measures ended at the end of 2022. At Chaldovar, entry time fell but costs rose from USD 8 to USD 44.

Construction of the China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan railway began on 27 December 2024. It is expected to cost USD 8 billion, mostly financed by China. The Kyrgyz Republic plans to contribute USD 130.5 million to the joint venture. Electrification is not planned.
paras.b: China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan railway: construction began in December 2024

paras.t: According to the OECD, the new railway will run from Kashgar via the Torugart Pass and Jalal-Abad to Andijan, and is expected to shorten transport from China to Europe by up to one week. The Kyrgyz Republic's total investment could reach USD 700 million (14.5% of the 2025 budget).
Underlying causes

The OECD cites a shortage and high cost of transit permits (dozvol), paper documents, inadequate border inspection equipment, rest areas and refrigeration, and empty return trips due to low eastbound freight. It recommends extending electronic permits and risk-based customs inspection to all borders.
paras.b: OECD: transit permits, paper documents and border facilities are issues

paras.t: OECD recommendations: make transit permit criteria transparent, lower their price and move to electronic permits; add terminals, inspection equipment and heated driver rest areas at border checkpoints; extend risk-based inspection and colour-coded lanes, including separate lanes for perishables, to all borders; align border operating hours with neighbours; and enable cargo insurance covering the whole corridor.
CAREC measurements show the road cost of 20 tonnes over 500 km swinging widely: USD 1,346 (2020), USD 2,194 (2021) and USD 1,888 (2022). Rail rose from USD 413 (2021) to USD 556 (2022).

The OECD states that, with customs' risk-based system, import and export clearance now takes 30 minutes from registration of the declaration and customs procedures at most 3 hours. Electronic queuing has started at Kyzyl-Kiya and Dostuk (Uzbek border). The country's average score on the OECD Trade Facilitation Indicators (2024) is 1.204, second in Central Asia after Kazakhstan.

On the other hand, the country joined the electronic consignment note (e-CMR) in 2022 and applied for electronic TIR (customs transit for international road transport) in April 2024, but neither is fully operational. More than 60% of respondents want customs declarations to be fully electronic.
Border reopening: the Kensai border crossing with Kazakhstan reopened at the end of 2024, and four border crossings with Tajikistan also reopened.

NDP 2030 lists railway electrification as a task, yet the largest new line is not planned to be electrified, and the relationship between the two is not explained. Railways are the first NDP 2030 target, yet the railway row has no active donor cooperation.
paras.b: New line not to be electrified; railway cooperation is a gap

paras.t: Related cooperation: the international corridors, borders and logistics row has 8 projects worth about USD 94.7 million (almost all ADB). The railway row has none.
paras.b: About USD 94.7 million in the corridors row (ADB); no railway projects

paras.t: Main border projects: ADB's border services improvement for the Almaty–Bishkek Economic Corridor (grant about USD 7.8 million, loan about USD 7.5 million, 2025–2030); ADB's preparation of CAREC transport connectivity (about USD 1 million); civil society's Ready4Trade (about USD 0.2 million); and Korea's integrated logistics centre (preparation stage).

Border times and costs depend more on procedures, permits and neighbouring countries' measures than on facilities. ADB's border services project covers both facilities and procedures. Institutional issues such as transit permits and electronic TIR offer large scope for technical cooperation.

sections.msg: Aviation has not returned to pre-COVID levels, and climate finance has begun to flow into the shift of urban transport to electric buses.

fig.cap: Figure 2-3 Passengers carried by Kyrgyz airlines

paras.t: Aviation

Passengers carried by Kyrgyz airlines fell from 1.18 million (2018) to 170,000–190,000 in 2020–21 and were 800,000 in 2023. The national target (7 million airport passengers) includes foreign airlines and cannot be compared with this figure.
paras.b: Domestic airline passengers: 800,000 (2023)

paras.t: Passengers on Kyrgyz airlines grew from 380,000 (2010) to 1.18 million (2018), fell to 870,000 in 2019, then collapsed with COVID-19.

The long-term strategy calls for modernising air traffic control and airspace in step with the renovation, expansion and construction of airports, and for upgrading radio, radar, navigation and communications equipment.
NDP 2030 lists removing domestic airlines from the ICAO "blacklist" as a tourism task.

NDP 2030's civil aviation tasks: expanding domestic and international routes; building, reconstructing and modernising airports; small aviation including private operators; modernising air navigation systems; flight safety and aviation security to international standards; unmanned aviation technology and regulation; and aviation human resource development.
The aviation row has one project: JICA's air traffic control facilities at international airports (about USD 15.4 million, 2024–2031).
paras.tnj: The aviation row has one project: air traffic control facilities at international airports.

paras.t: Urban transport
For urban transport, NDP 2030 lists electric and hybrid buses, a charging network and cycle lanes.

Related cooperation: the urban transport and e-mobility row has 3 projects worth about USD 42.5 million (Green Climate Fund e-mobility about USD 32.5 million, EBRD Bishkek buses about USD 9 million). The aviation row has 1 project worth about USD 15.4 million (JICA air traffic control facilities).
paras.b: About USD 42.5 million for urban transport; about USD 15.4 million for aviation
paras.tnj: Related cooperation: the urban transport and e-mobility row has 3 projects worth about USD 42.5 million (Green Climate Fund e-mobility about USD 32.5 million, EBRD Bishkek buses about USD 9 million). The aviation row has 1 project.
paras.bnj: About USD 42.5 million for urban transport

paras.t: Main urban transport projects: the Green Climate Fund e-mobility programme (about USD 32.5 million, 2024–2029); EBRD Bishkek buses (about USD 9 million); and ADB's preparation of additional financing for urban transport electrification (about USD 1 million). ADB's urban transport electrification (loan and grant of about USD 6.3 million each) ended in June 2026.

Data caveat: EBRD's Osh electric public transport (about USD 5.3 million) and Korea's electric vehicle and charging pilot (about USD 0.4 million) are not mapped to the urban transport row in the site's data.
The OECD recommends supporting low-emission road transport, for example by improving fuel quality. The World Bank assessment lists public transport as one of the areas where PPPs are active.

In urban transport, climate finance and EBRD are funding the shift to electric buses in Bishkek and Osh, a new donor trend. Because the text of the national plan has not been confirmed, it is not possible to tell which targets these projects serve.

The Green Climate Fund (about USD 32.5 million) and EBRD (about USD 32.9 million) are in urban transport and ring roads. EBRD funds the Issyk-Kul Ring Road (about USD 23.9 million) and Bishkek buses (about USD 9 million).

Closing dates of main projects: the Islamic Development Bank's Susamyr–Talas–Taraz road and ADB's CAREC Corridors 1 and 3 Connector Road at the end of 2027, ADB's border services in 2030, and ADB's Issyk-Kul Ring Road in 2033.

Two large trunk road projects end at the end of 2027. Whether their successors go to new sections of international corridors or to maintaining the domestic road network will shape the 50% roads target and the condition of domestic roads.

The World Bank assessment states that the national public investment programme amounts to only 3–5% of GDP a year, far below the needs for roads and other infrastructure. External funding for transport is expected to rise with year-to-year fluctuations, and donor loans are at the centre of road investment.

paras.t: Many Islamic Development Bank road projects began in the 2000s and were recorded as completed in June 2026 (phases of the Taraz–Talas–Suusamyr road, the Osh–Irkeshtam road, the Bishkek–Torugart road, etc.).

Funding over the past decade concentrated on three corridors: Bishkek–Osh (north–south), Bishkek–Torugart (China) and Talas (Kazakhstan). The improvement in international road condition shown in the Concept's tables appears to be the result of this concentration.
Data caveat: the about USD 22.5 million of completed World Bank projects is included in the aggregation used for the site but does not appear in the project-by-project list.
Funding has been and remains concentrated in trunk roads. New areas starting to receive funding are urban transport electrification and border services improvement.
paras.b: Funding consistently goes to trunk roads; new flows go to electrification and borders

paras.t: In urban transport, ADB's urban transport electrification (2021–2026) has ended, and ADB's preparation of additional financing (about USD 1 million, 2025–2029) has begun. The completed urban transport row has 5 projects worth about USD 12.5 million.

Apart from the "successful" rating of ADB's Bishkek–Torugart road, evaluations of completed projects have not been read this time. On the maintenance of rehabilitated roads, the World Bank assessment only expresses concern; project-by-project ex post checks are needed.

sections.msg: Railways are the only area with no active cooperation, though maintenance and institutions and finance have few dedicated projects.

fig.cap: Table 3-3 Strategy areas × donors (toggle active / completed / cumulative)

paras.t: Areas with no active cooperation: railways.
paras.b: Gap: railways

paras.t: Cooperation addressing the inefficient maintenance and funding shortfalls that the Concept cites as causes of road deterioration is limited to items such as maintenance equipment; most projects are new construction or rehabilitation.
paras.b: Maintenance and institutions and finance are thinly covered

paras.t: Of the Concept's pillars, maintenance and road safety (Pillar 4) and institutions and finance (Pillar 5) are counted together with the trunk roads row in the site's table. As a result, the amount of cooperation for maintenance and institutions cannot be separated out from the table.

Railways are the only empty row in the table, but in terms of where funding goes, maintenance, road safety, institution building and regional and local roads are thinly covered. Toll-road financing for maintenance, cited by the long-term strategy, is also not addressed by cooperation.
The railway row has no projects, either active or completed since 2017. Bridges, tunnels and passes, and aviation, also have no projects completed since 2017.

Railways are the first NDP 2030 target, and besides the China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan railway, electrification and rolling stock renewal are also listed as tasks, yet no multilateral donor cooperation can be found. Railway operations, safety and human resources offer entry points for technical cooperation.

sections.msg: Road investment continues, but the weight of national targets has shifted to railways, logistics and aviation, for which there are neither metrics nor plans.

paras.t: None of the five NDP 2030 targets can be tracked with annual published figures. A system to publish rail tonnage, airport passengers and the share of roads rehabilitated every year is needed first.
paras.b: A system to measure the five targets is needed first

paras.t: Donor funding is concentrated in trunk roads and does not adequately reach the deterioration of domestic roads or the rise in road traffic deaths. The results of maintenance reform (corporatisation) are the next issue.
paras.b: The results of maintenance reform are the next issue

paras.t: Large ADB and Islamic Development Bank road projects end at the end of 2027. How far successor projects cover domestic network maintenance, road safety and life-cycle cost planning will shape the indicators for domestic road condition and road deaths.

Both the long-term strategy and NDP 2030 name PPPs as a main instrument. Making PPPs work requires feasibility studies, contract supervision and regulation, and the World Bank assessment points to weaknesses precisely there (optional feasibility studies, an unused preparation fund).
Border procedures and transit permits are institutional rather than infrastructure problems, offering large scope for technical cooperation.
paras.b: Borders and transit permits offer scope for institutional technical cooperation

paras.t: PPPs have started in roads, railways and public transport, but project preparation funds remain largely unused. Reforms making life-cycle costs and feasibility studies mandatory would raise the quality of both PPPs and donor projects.

To watch next quarter: construction progress on the China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan railway, implementation reports on the road Concept, new road traffic death figures, and new border digitalisation moves.
paras.b: New railway, road implementation reports, road deaths, border digitalisation

paras.t: Also to watch next quarter: successors to ADB's CAREC Corridors 1 and 3 Connector Road and the Islamic Development Bank's Susamyr–Talas–Taraz road (due to end at the end of 2027), and progress in introducing electric buses in Bishkek and Osh.
